dtv_hero_lead: The Destination Thailand Visa lets you live in Chiang Mai with Muay Thai training as your qualifying activity — up to 5 years, 180 days per entry. We provide the training documents that support your application.
dtv_intro_p1: The Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) is Thailand's 5-year, multiple-entry visa for remote workers and people joining Thai soft-power activities — including Muay Thai training. Each entry lets you stay up to 180 days, extendable once.
dtv_intro_p2: Training at a recognised gym counts as a qualifying activity. That's where we come in: enrol in a long-term program at Wildcat and we provide the paperwork your application needs.
dtv_step1_b: Pick a monthly or multi-month training plan at Wildcat — your qualifying soft-power activity.
dtv_step2_b: We provide your enrolment letter and training confirmation, ready for your application.
dtv_step3_b: Apply at a Thai embassy or via e-visa, then make Chiang Mai home — up to 5 years.
dtv_inc1_b: Official confirmation of your long-term enrolment, issued by the gym.
dtv_inc2_b: Proof of ongoing training for extensions and re-entries.
dtv_inc3_b: Stay mobile during your season — rental available on site.
dtv_inc4_b: Accommodation pointers, local tips and a community from day one.
dtv_elig_body: Most applicants need a passport, proof of funds (around 500,000 THB) and a qualifying activity — that's your Muay Thai enrolment. Requirements vary by embassy; message us and we'll point you in the right direction for your situation.
dtv_faq_q1: How long can I stay on a DTV?
dtv_faq_a1: The visa is valid 5 years, multiple entry. Each entry allows up to 180 days, extendable once for another 180 days inside Thailand.
dtv_faq_q2: Does Muay Thai training really qualify?
dtv_faq_a2: Yes — Muay Thai is one of Thailand's recognised soft-power activities. A long-term enrolment at a gym like Wildcat is your qualifying activity.
dtv_faq_a3: An enrolment letter and a training confirmation matching your program. The rest (passport, proof of funds, application) stays on your side — we'll guide you through it.
dtv_faq_q4: How much money do I need to show?
dtv_faq_a4: Embassies generally ask for proof of around 500,000 THB in savings. Exact requirements vary by embassy — check the one where you'll apply.
dtv_faq_a5: At a Thai embassy or consulate outside Thailand, or online via the official Thai e-visa system, depending on your country.

classes_beg_meta_title: Beginner Muay Thai Classes in Thailand — First Class Guide
classes_beg_meta_desc: Beginner Muay Thai classes explained by a Chiang Mai camp owner: what your first session really feels like, what to wear and bring — no experience needed.
classes_beg_hero_title_em: what to expect at our Chiang Mai camp
classes_beg_hero_lead: You don't need any experience to start. You don't need to be fit. And nobody is putting you in the ring to fight on day one. That's not how a first class works here, no matter what the words “fight camp” made you picture.
classes_beg_author: By Meaw Boonpradub — owner of Wildcat Muay Thai, Chiang Mai. I've welcomed hundreds of first-timers to our garden ring.
classes_beg_intro_p1: This is the page I wish every nervous first-timer could read before they walk in. It's an honest, minute-by-minute look at what a beginner Muay Thai class actually feels like at our camp: arriving, the warm-up, your first basic moves, hitting pads with a coach, and the soreness that shows up the next day. I'll also cover what to wear, what to bring, and what your first few weeks really look like.
classes_beg_link_pillar: all our classes, schedule and prices
classes_beg_walk_title: What to expect in your first beginner Muay Thai class
classes_beg_walk_intro: Your first session breaks into five simple parts: you arrive and settle in, you warm up, you learn a few basic moves, you hit pads with a coach, and you stretch out. No surprises, no test, no pressure. Here's how each part actually goes.
classes_beg_walk1_p1: You'll feel the open air before anything else. We train outdoors, under a roof, with the garden and the ring right there, not a windowless studio. When you arrive, you'll often see a quick wai (hands together, a small bow) as a greeting; you don't need to get it perfect, just return it with a smile. Drop your bag at the side, grab your water, and find a spot near the ring.
classes_beg_walk1_p2: One honest note: Chiang Mai is hot, and we train in that heat. Come hydrated, and bring more water than you think you need. The warmth is part of why training here feels different, but your body needs a beat to settle into it.
classes_beg_walk2_p1: This is where most first-timers are caught off guard: you'll sweat, a lot, before you've thrown a single punch. The warm-up is usually skipping rope, light jogging or shadow movement, then some mobility work. It wakes up the joints you're about to use.
classes_beg_walk2_p2: Go at your own pace. If the rope trips you up for the first ten minutes, that's normal. Half the room was there once. Nobody is counting your mistakes. You're warming up, not auditioning.
classes_beg_walk3_p1: In your first beginner class you'll learn a small handful of basic moves, not the whole sport. Expect your stance and guard first, then a jab and a cross, a teep (the front push-kick), and a basic low kick. That's plenty for one session.
classes_beg_walk3_p2: We keep it light on purpose. The deep technical breakdown comes with reps over weeks, not in a wall of instructions on day one. Learn the shape of the movement, repeat it slowly, and let it feel awkward. That awkward stage is everyone's starting point.
classes_beg_walk4_p1: This is the part people fall in love with. You hold up your hands, your coach holds the Thai pads, and you throw the combinations you just learned while they call them out and correct you on the spot, usually with a grin. Even in a group class, those few minutes on the pads are one-on-one. It's just you and a Thai coach who has taught total beginners for years.
classes_beg_walk4_p2: This is where it clicks that Muay Thai is something you do, not something you watch. Want to know who'll be holding the pads?
classes_beg_walk5_p1: You'll finish with a stretch and a breather. Then comes the part nobody warns you about: the next-day soreness. Your shins, your shoulders, maybe muscles you forgot you had. That's completely normal after a first session, and it fades fast as your body adapts.
classes_beg_walk5_p2: How soon should you come back? Most beginners do well with two or three sessions in their first week, with a rest day between. You don't have to train twice a day to make progress. That rhythm is there if you want it, but it isn't the entry fee.
classes_beg_wear_title: What to wear and bring to Muay Thai class
classes_beg_wear_intro: You almost certainly own everything you need already. Here's the short list for what to wear to Muay Thai as a beginner:
classes_beg_wear_li1: Sports shorts and a breathable t-shirt. You don't need real Muay Thai shorts to start.
classes_beg_wear_li2: A water bottle, bigger than you'd bring to a normal gym, because of the heat.
classes_beg_wear_li3: A small towel. You'll want it.
classes_beg_wear_li4: Boxing gloves are lent by the camp for your first sessions, so you don't need to buy a pair to try.
classes_beg_wear_li5: Bare feet on the ring. You train without shoes, so no special footwear.
classes_beg_wear_outro: A few Thailand-specific notes: the heat and humidity are real, so hydrate before and during. If you're training a daytime session in the open air, a little sunscreen doesn't hurt. And go easy on a heavy meal beforehand: train on a light stomach.

classes_beg_fit_title: Do you need to be fit to start?
classes_beg_fit_p1: No. This is the single biggest fear I see, and it's the easiest one to put to rest. You do not need to be fit to start Muay Thai as a beginner. You get fit by training, not before it.
classes_beg_fit_p2: We adapt the intensity to you. People of every age, shape and fitness level start here: solo travellers, complete beginners who've never thrown a kick, folks who haven't exercised in years. What I see every week is simple: the people who were most nervous walking in are often the ones grinning by the cool-down. The only bad first class is the one you never take.
classes_beg_fit_p3: Worried about coming alone? Solo travellers, women training on their own, and teens are all genuinely welcome. It's a family-run camp, and that's not a slogan. If you want a gentler on-ramp or have questions before you book, just ask.
classes_beg_th_title: Starting Muay Thai in Thailand vs back home
classes_beg_th_intro: Starting Muay Thai in Thailand as a beginner is easier than starting back home, not harder. That surprises people who expected an intimidating fight camp. Here's why it's friendlier:
classes_beg_th_li1_t: Thai coaches teach beginners every single day.
classes_beg_th_li1_b: It's their craft. You're not an inconvenience between “serious” fighters; teaching newcomers is the job.
classes_beg_th_li2_b: You can drop in for one class. If you love it, you come back. If you don't, you've lost nothing but an hour and some sweat.
classes_beg_th_li3_t: The cost per session is far lower than in the West.
classes_beg_th_li3_b: A single drop-in here costs a fraction of a Western gym's monthly fee.
classes_beg_th_li4_t: You can train as often as you like.
classes_beg_th_li4_b: Once a week or every day, the camp is open and the choice is yours.
classes_beg_th_etiq: There's a little culture to learn, and it's simple. The wai is a respectful greeting. You don't wear shoes on the ring, and you treat the ring and the coaches with respect. You'll pick it up by watching, no lessons required. That's the whole etiquette lesson.

classes_beg_weeks_title: Your first weeks: how fast will you progress?
classes_beg_weeks_p1: Honest timeline: your first class is about surviving the warm-up and learning a few shapes, and that's a win. By week two or three, basic combinations start to flow without you thinking through every step. Over the first one to three months, real technique begins to settle in.
classes_beg_weeks_p2a: There's no magic number, and anyone promising you'll “master Muay Thai in 30 days” is selling something. Progress comes from showing up. Two or three sessions a week, checked against
classes_beg_weeks_p2b: , will take a complete beginner a long way.
classes_beg_weeks_cta_lead: Come try a class. The first one's easy to book.
classes_beg_faq_q1: Is Muay Thai good for beginners?
classes_beg_faq_a1: Yes. It's built to be learned in stages, and a beginner class is structured around that: warm-up, a few basic moves, pad work, cool-down. You start with the fundamentals and add from there. No prior martial arts experience needed.
classes_beg_faq_q2: Is Muay Thai hard to learn?
classes_beg_faq_a2: Honestly: it's physically demanding, but technically simple at the start. The first moves (stance, jab, cross, teep) are easy to grasp and hard to master, which is the fun of it. The difficulty scales up as you do, so it never feels out of reach on day one.
classes_beg_faq_q3: How long does it take to learn Muay Thai?
classes_beg_faq_a3: You'll have the basic moves within a few weeks of regular training, and real comfort in your combinations within a few months. “Learning Muay Thai” never fully ends, but you'll feel competent far sooner than you'd expect. There's no fixed number, just consistent reps.
classes_beg_faq_q4: Can I just drop in for one class in Chiang Mai?
classes_beg_faq_a4: Yes. You can drop in for a single beginner Muay Thai class in Chiang Mai with no commitment and no contract. The drop-in rate is public on our classes page. Come once, see how it feels, decide from there.

The best gym is the one that fits you.

dtv_apply_step2_b: Create an account on the official Thai e-Visa portal at thaievisa.go.th. It's the only official site — don't pay a third-party 'portal' that claims to do it for you.
dtv_apply_step3_t: Select the DTV and your category
dtv_apply_step3_b: Choose the Destination Thailand Visa and select your qualifying category: Workcation, Thai Soft Power, or Dependent. Muay Thai sits under the Soft Power category — this is the route we prepare documents for.
dtv_apply_step4_b: Prepare your passport (valid 6+ months, blank pages), a 4×6 cm photo, 3 to 6 months of bank statements showing 500,000 THB or equivalent income, proof of accommodation and a travel plan, and health insurance with around $50,000 USD of medical coverage (required by some embassies — confirm yours). Wildcat: we provide your signed enrolment letter, training schedule and paid receipt. Use the interactive checklist below to track every document.
dtv_apply_step5_b: Complete the online DTV application form on the portal — your personal details, your chosen category and the document uploads.
dtv_apply_step6_t: Upload documents and pay the fee
dtv_apply_step6_b: Upload your documents as PDF or JPEG and pay the 10,000 THB application fee online. The fee is non-refundable, even if the application is rejected. Wildcat: our camp documents come as clean PDFs, ready to upload.
dtv_apply_step7_t: Wait for processing, then enter Thailand
dtv_apply_step7_b: Processing usually takes 5 to 15 business days (longer, up to around 3 to 6 weeks, in high season). Once you're approved you get an email, and you can enter Thailand for up to 180 days per stay, with a 5-year multiple-entry validity. If you're staying long-term to train, message us your arrival date and we'll have your first session ready.

dtv_apply_mistakes_title: Common mistakes that get DTV applications rejected
dtv_apply_mistakes_intro: This is what I actually see go wrong. None of it is about luck — it's about a clean, consistent file.
dtv_apply_mistake1: Applying from inside Thailand. The DTV is applied for from abroad — doing it from inside the country gets the application rejected.
dtv_apply_mistake2: Inconsistent funds. The 500,000 THB that appears the day before, or erratic movements across the 3–6 months of statements, raises questions. Keep your funds steady and visible.
dtv_apply_mistake3: Weak or generic activity documents: a letter from an unregistered camp, no training schedule, a missing receipt. This is exactly what we fix — real, signed camp documents from a registered Muay Thai camp.
dtv_apply_mistake4: A passport with less than 6 months of validity, or no blank pages left.
dtv_apply_mistake5: No health insurance when the embassy requires it — check your embassy's rules before you submit.
dtv_apply_mistake6: Believing a paid 'agent portal' is the official site. There's only one: thaievisa.go.th.

dtv_faqp_q1: What is the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV)?
dtv_faqp_a1: The DTV is a 5-year, multiple-entry Thailand visa that lets you stay up to 180 days per entry. It's built for remote workers (“Workcation”) and people doing recognised Thai soft-power activities like Muay Thai, Thai cooking or medical treatment. You apply once and use it over five years.
dtv_faqp_q2: Who is eligible for the DTV visa?
dtv_faqp_a2: Anyone who fits one of three categories: remote workers and freelancers for foreign employers (Workcation), participants in Thai soft-power activities (Muay Thai, cooking, medical care, festivals), or dependents of a DTV holder. You also need to show 500,000 THB in funds. The specific paperwork depends on your category.
dtv_faqp_q3: Which countries can apply for the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a3: The DTV is open to most nationalities — there's no short “eligible countries” list the way some visas have. What changes by country is where and how you apply (your nearest Thai embassy or consulate, or the e-Visa portal) and sometimes the exact documents requested. Always confirm with the embassy you'll apply at.
dtv_faqp_q4: What are the DTV soft-power categories (Muay Thai, cooking, medical)?
dtv_faqp_a4: “Soft power” covers the Thai cultural and wellness activities the government wants to promote — Muay Thai training, Thai cooking courses, medical treatment, sports and festivals. For each, you show you're genuinely enrolled or booked. For Muay Thai, that means a long-term enrolment at a camp.
dtv_faqp_q5: Do I qualify for the DTV through Muay Thai training?
dtv_faqp_a5: Yes — Muay Thai is one of Thailand's recognised soft-power activities, so a long-term enrolment at a camp is a qualifying activity. You support it with an enrolment or training letter from the camp. See our full Muay Thai soft-power guide for what immigration looks for.
dtv_faqp_q6: What is a soft-power acceptance or enrolment letter, and who issues it?
dtv_faqp_a6: It's a letter from your camp or school confirming you're enrolled in a long-term Muay Thai program — one of the documents that backs your soft-power application. The camp issues it; at Wildcat, Meaw prepares it to match your actual training plan. It supports your file but doesn't replace the other requirements (funds, passport, application).
dtv_faqp_q7: Is the DTV easy to get? What are common denial reasons?
dtv_faqp_a7: For a well-prepared file it's a straightforward visa, but it's not automatic. The denials we hear about usually come from weak proof of funds (money that just appeared, with no history), a soft-power or remote-work activity that looks thin or generic, or inconsistent documents. Honest answer: a clean, consistent file is everything.
dtv_faqp_q8: Is there a minimum age for the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a8: The main applicant must be an adult (18+). Children can come as dependents on a DTV Dependent visa. Check the exact rule with your embassy if a minor would be the main applicant.
dtv_faqp_q9: How much money do I need in the bank for the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a9: You need to show 500,000 THB (roughly USD 14,500–17,000) in a bank statement. This is the financial requirement across categories. It proves you can support yourself during long stays.
dtv_faqp_q10: How long must the 500,000 THB sit in my account?
dtv_faqp_a10: Plan for the money to be there with some history, not deposited the day before you apply. Exact seasoning periods aren't fixed publicly and embassies read statements differently — a stable balance over several months is the safe read. When in doubt, ask the embassy you'll apply at.
dtv_faqp_q11: Can a sponsor in Thailand cover the funds requirement?
dtv_faqp_a11: Honest answer: it depends on the embassy and category, so don't assume yes. Some posts accept a sponsorship letter plus the sponsor's funds; others want the money in the applicant's own account. Confirm before you build your file around a sponsor.
dtv_faqp_q12: How much does the DTV visa cost?
dtv_faqp_a12: The visa fee is around USD 400 (about 10,000 THB), though it varies by embassy. That's separate from the funds you show and from any in-country extension fee. Budget for the fee per applicant.
dtv_faqp_q13: How do I apply for the DTV visa?
dtv_faqp_a13: You apply online through Thailand's official e-Visa portal (thaievisa.go.th) from outside Thailand — create an account, upload your documents, and pay the fee. Some applicants use their nearest Thai embassy or consulate. See our step-by-step how-to-apply guide for the full walkthrough.
dtv_faqp_q14: Do I apply from outside Thailand?
dtv_faqp_a14: Yes. The DTV must be applied for from outside Thailand — you can't convert to it from inside the country on the same trip. Plan to apply before you travel, or on a trip home.
dtv_faqp_q15: What documents do I need for the DTV application?
dtv_faqp_a15: A passport, proof of 500,000 THB in funds, and documents for your category — for Muay Thai, your camp enrolment or training letter; for Workcation, proof of remote work. Exact lists vary by embassy and category. We provide the training documents; the rest stays on your side and we guide you through it.
dtv_faqp_q16: How long does DTV processing take?
dtv_faqp_a16: It varies a lot — from a few days to several weeks — depending on the embassy and how complete your file is. There's no single official figure. A complete, consistent file is the best way to keep it short.
dtv_faqp_q17: Why does processing time vary so much between embassies?
dtv_faqp_a17: Each Thai embassy or consulate handles its own DTV workload and applies the document rules slightly differently. Busy posts are slower; some request extra paperwork. That's why we tell people to check their specific embassy's page and apply with margin before they want to travel.
dtv_faqp_q18: Do I need a visa agent for the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a18: No — many people apply themselves through the e-Visa portal. The real value isn't an agent, it's getting your category documents right; for the Muay Thai route, that's where the camp comes in. We're not a visa agency — we give you the training documents and guide you, and you keep control of your own file.
dtv_faqp_q19: How long can I stay per entry on the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a19: Up to 180 days per entry. The visa itself is valid 5 years with multiple entries, so you can come and go across those five years. Each fresh entry starts a new 180-day stay.
dtv_faqp_q20: What happens after 180 days — can I extend?
dtv_faqp_a20: You can extend once inside Thailand for another 180 days (extension fee around 1,900 THB), or do a visa run. After that you reset by leaving and re-entering. Extensions are handled by Thai immigration.
dtv_faqp_q21: What is a visa run, and how does it reset my stay?
dtv_faqp_a21: A visa run is simply leaving Thailand and re-entering on your still-valid DTV, which starts a fresh 180-day stay. Because the DTV is multiple-entry for 5 years, you can do this throughout its validity. Plan trips that make sense, not back-to-back border bounces.
dtv_faqp_q22: Do I need a re-entry permit with the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a22: No — the DTV is multiple-entry, so you don't need a separate re-entry permit to leave and come back during its validity. That's one of its big advantages over single-entry long-stay visas.
dtv_faqp_q23: How do I keep my DTV active across the 5 years?
dtv_faqp_a23: Keep the visa valid by using it within its 5-year window and respecting each 180-day stay (extend, or exit and re-enter as needed). Rules around long-stay visas do change, so check current requirements before each trip — that's why we keep this page's review date current.
dtv_faqp_q24: Will I owe Thai tax on the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a24: Maybe — it depends on how long you stay and whether you bring foreign income into Thailand. Spending 180+ days in a calendar year makes you a Thai tax resident, which can create Thai tax obligations on income remitted to Thailand. This is general info, not tax advice — talk to a tax professional about your situation.
dtv_faqp_q25: Does the 180-day rule make me a Thai tax resident?
dtv_faqp_a25: Yes — 180 days or more in a calendar year in Thailand makes you a tax resident for that year, separate from your visa's 180-day-per-entry stay limit. They're two different “180s.” Tax residency can mean filing and paying Thai tax on certain income.
dtv_faqp_q26: Do I still have to file taxes back home (e.g. US)?
dtv_faqp_a26: Usually yes — your home-country obligations don't disappear because you're on the DTV. US citizens, for example, generally still file (FEIE and FBAR may apply). Check your own country's rules — this isn't tax advice; speak to a cross-border tax professional.
dtv_faqp_q27: Can I bring my spouse and children on the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a27: Yes — your spouse and children under 20 can apply as dependents on linked DTV Dependent visas. Each dependent files their own application with their own fee. You'll show proof of relationship.
dtv_faqp_q28: Do dependents need their own work or funds documents?
dtv_faqp_a28: Dependents don't need their own remote-work or soft-power activity — they qualify through their relationship to you. Whether each dependent must also show funds, or whether the main applicant's 500,000 THB covers the family, can vary — confirm with your embassy.
dtv_faqp_q29: Can I work in Thailand on the DTV?
dtv_faqp_a29: You can work remotely for foreign employers or clients — that's the whole point of the Workcation category. You cannot take a Thai job, work for Thai companies, or invoice Thai clients, and you don't get a Thai work permit. The DTV is not a work-permit visa.
dtv_faqp_q30: Is the DTV the right visa for a multi-month Muay Thai trip?
dtv_faqp_a30: For a serious multi-month training stay, the DTV is usually the best fit — 180 days per entry, 5-year validity, and Muay Thai is a qualifying soft-power activity. We help you with the training documents and guide your file. Plan your stay with our long-stay training guide.

dtv_lst_week_body: Most long-stay trainees run two sessions a day — a technical morning and a harder evening on pads, bag, and clinch — five to six days a week, with Sunday off. Sparring stays progressive, and the vibe is open-air garden and pool, not a dark gym. Every level is welcome, from your first day to fight-ready.
dtv_lst_progress_title: How your body and skill progress over months
dtv_lst_progress_body: Weeks one to four are adaptation: sore legs, conditioning, and the basics of stance and rhythm. Months two and three add volume, real clinch work, and your first controlled sparring. From month four onward, trainees who want it can look at a local fight — a possibility we help with, never a promise.
dtv_lst_who_title: Who comes for the long haul
dtv_lst_who_body: Traveling athletes, people between chapters, and remote workers who pair their laptop with two sessions a day. You will train under our Thai coaches alongside fighters who came up here.
dtv_lst_budget_title: The real monthly budget, broken down
dtv_lst_budget_intro: Here is the cost of training in Chiang Mai, line by line. Training prices are our real public rates; everything else is a typical Chiang Mai range for planning.
dtv_lst_training_body: For a long stay, the monthly unlimited pass is your baseline; the fighter program is the step up if you train twice a day, every day. Our full public training rates live on the classes page.
dtv_lst_accom_body: A basic studio near the camp runs about 6,000–9,000 THB a month; a comfort condo with pool and gym lands around 14,000–20,000 THB. Camp-room availability varies — ask us, or see the Stay & Train page for accommodation-included packages.
dtv_lst_food_body: Eating mostly Thai street food (around 60 THB a meal) keeps you near 6,000 THB a month; leaning western pushes you toward 15,000 THB.
dtv_lst_scooter_body: A rented scooter is about 3,000 THB a month, plus petrol — the standard way to get to the camp and around Chiang Mai.
dtv_lst_extras_body: Budget roughly 2,000 THB a month for gear, recovery massage, a SIM, insurance, and a little leisure — more if you travel on rest days.
dtv_lst_total_title: Putting it together: a ~33,000–35,000 THB monthly floor
dtv_lst_total_body: Add it up and a disciplined full-time month starts around 33,000–35,000 THB. Long-stay discounts of 20–40% are common on training, so the longer you stay, the lower your real number — message us for a rate.
dtv_lst_cities_title: Chiang Mai vs Phuket vs Bangkok
dtv_lst_cities_body: Of the three, Chiang Mai is the most affordable. Phuket camps run pricier and the island lifts your cost of living; Bangkok studio rents push your budget up fast. For a long haul on a budget, Chiang Mai gives the best balance of training and price.
dtv_lst_legal_title: How the DTV makes a long stay legal
dtv_lst_legal_body: The DTV (Destination Thailand Visa) runs up to five years, with 180 days per entry, and Muay Thai training counts as a qualifying soft-power activity. Wildcat provides the training documents that support your file. Plan for the 500,000 THB proof-of-funds requirement as a budget line — we keep the process itself on the visa pages.

dtv_lst_faq_q1: How much does it cost to train Muay Thai in Thailand per month?
dtv_lst_faq_a1: A full-time month in Chiang Mai — training, a room, food, and a scooter — runs about 33,000–35,000 THB. Use the estimator above to plan your own number, since accommodation and lifestyle move the total.
dtv_lst_faq_q2: Is Chiang Mai or Phuket cheaper for Muay Thai training?
dtv_lst_faq_a2: Chiang Mai. Phuket's camps tend to charge more and the island's cost of living is higher, so the same month costs noticeably less in Chiang Mai.
dtv_lst_faq_q3: How much money do you need to live and train for a year?
dtv_lst_faq_a3: Budget roughly 33,000–35,000 THB a month across twelve months, and plan for the DTV's 500,000 THB proof-of-funds requirement on top. Long-stay discounts usually bring the monthly figure down.

dtv_lst_faq_a4: Yes — long-stay discounts of 20–40% are common on training. The exact rate depends on how long you commit, so message us for your number.

dtv_mt_hero_title: Muay Thai visa in Thailand: DTV vs ED visa —
dtv_mt_hero_lead: Want to train Muay Thai in Thailand for months, not weeks? Here's how the DTV and the ED visa really compare — and the training documents we issue here at Wildcat in Chiang Mai.
dtv_mt_bluf: There's no visa literally called a "Muay Thai visa." For most foreign trainees today, the right long-stay route is the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) — a 5-year, multiple-entry visa that lets you live in Thailand 180 days per entry, with Muay Thai as your qualifying soft-power activity. The older ED (education) visa still fits a narrow case: deep, full-time, single-gym immersion. This page compares both honestly, then shows the training documents we issue here in Chiang Mai.
dtv_mt_disclaimer: Immigration rules change, and the final decision always rests with the Thai embassy or consulate you apply to. This guide reflects how we help trainees prepare their files at our Chiang Mai camp — it isn't legal advice. Always confirm current requirements with an official Thai mission before you apply.

dtv_mt_soft_title: Is there really a "Muay Thai visa"?
dtv_mt_soft_p1: Not as a named visa. What people call a Muay Thai visa is really the DTV, with Muay Thai listed as a qualifying activity. Since the DTV launched, Muay Thai counts as an eligible Thai soft-power activity — one of the cultural and sport categories Thailand actively wants visitors to come and do, alongside Thai cooking and other traditions.
dtv_mt_soft_p2: This is the part most camps don't explain. Understanding that your training is the legal basis of the application — your qualifying activity — is exactly what lets you fill the file in correctly the first time.

dtv_mt_faq_q1: Do I need prior Muay Thai experience to get the visa?
dtv_mt_faq_a1: No. Beginners are welcome — what matters for the file is that you're genuinely enrolled in a training program, not your level. We help complete beginners just as often as experienced fighters.
dtv_mt_faq_q2: Can I work remotely while on a Muay Thai DTV?
dtv_mt_faq_a2: Yes. The DTV is designed for remote workers and people joining Thai soft-power activities, so combining Muay Thai training with remote work is exactly what it's for.
dtv_mt_faq_q3: Do I have to keep training at the same gym after approval?
dtv_mt_faq_a3: No. Unlike the ED visa, the DTV doesn't lock you to one gym. After approval you're free to change camps, travel and train anywhere in Thailand.
dtv_mt_faq_q4: Is the ED visa or the DTV better if I want to fight?
dtv_mt_faq_a4: For most fighters the DTV wins: it's flexible, longer and lets you travel for fights. The ED visa only really makes sense if you want full-time, single-gym immersion and don't mind the in-country admin.
